description: A team of close friends who have been doing projects together for a long time
summary:
We built Lunar Site Planner, a web app that helps anyone choose where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. For any site and date it shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon from NASA LOLA data and answers two questions: will the lander have sunlight for power, and Earth in view for radio? It gives a GO / GO WITH CARE / NO GO verdict, sunset and Earthset countdowns, power and Deep Space Network estimates, finds the best landing spots and compares launch slips. Positions match NASA JPL Horizons to under 0.01°.

Our first version put everything on one dense screen, and testing showed it was as overwhelming as the expert tools the challenge describes. So we redesigned around people. Inspired by Duolingo, Beginner mode is a calm one-step-at-a-time walk with our guide Lumi, with a "why" only when you want it. Inspired by Apple, Professional mode keeps every tool in a clean interface with a spotlight tour. Unlike most planning tools, one app serves both students and mission planners.

This matters because launch delays force teams to re-check power and communications fast, and everyone affected should understand that decision.
details:
THE PROBLEM WE SAW

Near the Moon's south pole the Sun skims the horizon and Earth bobs in and out of view, so a ridge a few kilometres away, or a launch slip of a few days, can decide whether a lander has power and radio contact. Tools like Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons hold the answers but are built for specialists. Our own first version had the same flaw: every number on one dense screen. Testing it, we realised it was overwhelming, so we redesigned the whole experience around people.

WHAT WE BUILT

Lunar Site Planner is a web app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. Pick one of 29 curated sites (Apollo, CLPS landers such as IM-1, IM-2 and Blue Ghost, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang'e, Luna, and best-lit points we computed from NASA LOLA terrain) or any coordinates, and any date. It shows where the Sun and Earth sit against the real local horizon and answers two questions: will the lander have sunlight for power, and will Earth be in view for a direct radio link?

TWO MODES, ONE ENGINE

- Beginner (inspired by Duolingo): a calm, one-step-at-a-time walk with our guide Lumi. Pick a place and a date, look around a 360° skyline of real terrain, get a GO / GO WITH CARE / NO GO verdict for power and for Earth contact, test a launch slip, and compare two places. Every step has an optional "Why does this happen?". Unlike most planning tools, it needs no prior knowledge.

- Professional (inspired by Apple's design): every tool on one clean screen. A 3D Moon with CAD-style (PTC Creo) controls, a live status pill, a 30-day to 1-year timeline, assessment panels, a south-pole sunlight map, and a Terrain 3D view (CesiumJS) with real LOLA relief and shadows. A spotlight tour blurs everything except the part being explained.

HOW IT WORKS

- Sun and Earth positions: Astronomy Engine ephemeris rotated into the Moon's body-fixed frame (IAU model). Checked against NASA JPL Horizons: Sun at Apollo 11 (1969) within 0.007°, Earth from the Shackleton ridge (2027) within 0.0001°, Sun at Reiner Gamma within 0.002°.

- Horizons: ray-traced through NASA LRO LOLA south-pole terrain grids (240 m). With no atmosphere, the terrain is the horizon.

- Outputs: solar elevation and visible fraction of the Sun's disk, solar power and battery need for a configurable lander, Earth clearance above terrain, a link budget to NASA's Deep Space Network, and countdowns to sunset and Earthset.

KEY FEATURES

- Best-spot finder: searches 59 candidates (curated sites plus the brightest cells of our 2027 LOLA sunlight map) and highlights the best spot overall and the best site a mission has already landed on, ranked by time with both sunlight and Earth in view, with dotted links to Earth.

- Built for schedule changes: compare the same site 1, 2 and 3 lunar months later, compare sites side by side, export CSV, and share a link that reopens the exact site and date.

- "Look: Earth" drops you onto the surface to watch Earth rise over the real lunar horizon.

- Narrated video tours, dark and light mode, keyboard support, works on phones, no login or install.

WHY IT MATTERS

When hardware or launch delays move a mission, teams must re-check power and communications fast. Our tool gives an answer a planner can trust and a student, teacher or member of the public can understand, so everyone affected can reason about the same decision.

HONEST LIMITS

Real terrain covers the south pole (south of about 75°S); elsewhere the Moon is treated as a smooth sphere. The 240 m grid makes ridge-top values approximate. The verdicts use our own rules of thumb. Earth is not to scale in 3D views.

HOW WE BUILT IT

Before the event we prototyped the calculation engine and an early expert dashboard. During the hackathon we redesigned the experience: the intro, Beginner mode with Lumi, the Professional interface, the best-spot finder, the Terrain 3D view and the video tours.

Tools: JavaScript, Vite, Three.js, CesiumJS, Tailwind CSS, Astronomy Engine; Python for data preparation; Playwright and FFmpeg for the videos. We used Claude Code (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant for code and text, and Kokoro text-to-speech for the video narration; both are labelled as SI-assisted. No NASA logos or branding are used.

DATA

NASA LRO LOLA terrain, NASA LRO LROC WAC Moon mosaics (via USGS Astrogeology), NASA Blue Marble, NASA Deep Space Network station locations, NASA JPL Horizons for validation.
